The propulsion system concept considered for the High-Speed Civil Transport (HSCT) was an underwing, dual-propulsion, pod-per-wing installation.
Adverse transient phenomena such as engine compressor stall and inlet unstart could severely degrade the performance of one of these propulsion pods.
The representative propulsion pod consisted of a two-dimensional, bifurcated inlet mated to a live turbojet engine.
The propulsion pod was mounted below a large flat plate that acted as a wing simulator, which was nominally 10 feet wide by 18 feet long.
Transient instrumentation, including static pressure taps and intrusive pressure probes, was used to document the aerodynamic flow-field conditions during an unstart sequence.
A typical unstart sequence disrupts the local flow field for only about 50 milliseconds, which was a significant technical challenge.
In addition to flow-field pressure data, the researchers also determined the transient flow angle and Mach number.
The comprehensive final report on this test program will be released during calendar year 2000.
The loss of thrust and increased drag from an engine compressor stall and inlet unstart could cause aircraft stability and control problems that could lead to a catastrophic accident.
The objective of the test program was to assess the underwing flow field of a High-Speed Civil Transport propulsion system during an engine compressor stall and subsequent inlet unstart.
The wind tunnel tests were conducted in the 10- by 10-Foot Supersonic Wind Tunnel at the NASA Glenn Research Center at Lewis Field.

This wind tunnel test program was a success, and for the first time, researchers acquired flow-field aerodynamic data during a supersonic propulsion system engine compressor stall and inlet unstart sequence.
Aircraft system engineers must understand these transient events to design effective control systems to avoid and/or alleviate their effects.
The long length of the wing simulator (18 feet) allowed realistic boundary layers to form at the inlet cowl plane.
The data from this test program are still being reduced, and a comprehensive final report will be released in 2000.
